title: Biosafety at the Bench: Cabinets, Sharps, HBV Exposure and Sentinel Referral
summary: Learn which work belongs in a biological safety cabinet, which isolates are red flags, what the OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard says about engineering controls and recapping, how a needlestick is managed in a vaccinated worker, and how sentinel laboratories rule out and refer possible select agents.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 57 Hits 19 (BSC containment for aerosol and high-risk work), 20 (OSHA engineering controls; recapping), 27 (needlestick in a vaccinated worker) and 48 (suspected select agent: BSC rule-out and referral; LRN tiers). Checked against the CDC Biosafety Blue Ribbon Panel guidelines (Miller 2012; CDC MMWR web page), the OSHA standard text (29 CFR 1910.1030, eCFR 2026-10-01), ACIP 2018 (Schillie 2018, PMC full text) and the CDC 2013 HCP guidance (Schillie 2013; CDC MMWR web page), and CDC LRN web pages. Qualifications: recapping has a narrow one-handed/mechanical exception (rv-osha-recap-exception); HBV management depends on documented response status and source HBsAg, and the low-titre response-unknown path is HBIG ×1 plus revaccination, not just a booster (rv-hbv-pep-vaccinated-hcp); all rules are US (rv-ch57-us-biosafety-scope). Not taught: Hit 47 select-agent morphology (B. anthracis, Y. pestis, Brucella features), Hit 18 labelling, HIV post-exposure prophylaxis.

objectives: Name laboratory procedures that generate aerosols and the isolate features that should keep work in a biological safety cabinet.
Apply the OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard on engineering controls, PPE and needle recapping.
Choose hepatitis B post-exposure management for a vaccinated health-care worker from response status and source HBsAg.
Describe the sentinel, reference and national tiers of the Laboratory Response Network.

scenes.title: One bottle, one needle
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a blood-culture bottle flags positive after about 3 days; the Gram stain shows tiny gram-negative coccobacilli. A processor taps the bottle with a needle and subcultures it on the open bench, then recaps the needle with two hands and sticks a finger. The processor finished a hepatitis B vaccine series years ago but never had anti-HBs checked; the source patient’s HBsAg status is unknown. Question token: “Bench or cabinet? Treat or test?”

cues.text: A blood culture turns positive after three days. The Gram stain shows tiny gram-negative coccobacilli, and a processor subcultures it on the open bench.
Then the processor recaps the needle with two hands and sticks a finger. The processor was vaccinated against hepatitis B years ago, but antibody was never checked.
Bench or cabinet? And after the stick, treat now or test first?

props.label: Bench or cabinet? Treat or test?

scenes.title: Aerosols, cabinets and red-flag isolates
scenes.altText: Schematic bench and Class II biological safety cabinet (BSC). Aerosol card (Miller 2012): aerosols can come from most routine procedures and are often undetectable — subculturing positive blood cultures, making smears, centrifuging, vortexing, pouring, opening containers, catalase tests, preparing isolates for automated identification. BSL card: at BSL-2 the BSC is used for specimen processing and work producing aerosols or splashes; at BSL-3 the BSC is used for work with all specimens and cultures. Red-flag card: indicators of a possible high-risk pathogen that keep work in the BSC — slowly growing tiny colonies at 24–48 h with gram-negative rods or coccobacilli; blood cultures positive at ≥48 h with small gram-negative rods or coccobacilli; growth only on chocolate agar; boxcar-shaped gram-positive rods. Closed-system analyzers reduce but do not eliminate exposure.

cues.text: Aerosols are often undetectable, and most routine steps can make them: subculturing blood-culture bottles, making smears, centrifuging, vortexing, pouring, opening containers, even a catalase test.
At biosafety level two, specimen processing and any work that can make aerosols or splashes go in the biological safety cabinet. At level three, all specimens and cultures are handled in it.

Some findings hint at a high-risk pathogen, so work stays in the cabinet: tiny, slow colonies of gram-negative rods or coccobacilli, blood cultures positive only after forty-eight hours with small gram-negative rods or coccobacilli, growth only on chocolate agar, or boxcar-shaped gram-positive rods.
Closed-system sampling on analyzers lowers the risk but does not remove it, so the outside of every blood tube is still treated as contaminated.

props.title: Red flags: stay in the BSC

props.label: Closed analyzers: lower risk, not zero

scenes.title: Sharps under the OSHA standard
scenes.altText: Hierarchy card (US OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030(d)(2)): engineering and work practice controls are used to eliminate or minimise exposure; PPE is added where exposure remains. Engineering card: controls that isolate or remove the hazard — sharps disposal containers, self-sheathing needles, sharps with engineered sharps injury protections, needleless systems. Recapping card ((d)(2)(vii)): contaminated needles and sharps are not bent, recapped or removed unless the employer shows no alternative is feasible or a specific procedure requires it — and then only by a mechanical device or one-handed technique; shearing or breaking is prohibited. Plan card: the exposure control plan is reviewed at least annually, documenting consideration of safer devices, with input from frontline staff. Exposure card ((f)(3)): after a reported exposure the employer makes a confidential medical evaluation immediately available, including testing the source person’s blood for HBV and HIV as soon as feasible after consent.

cues.text: Under the US OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard, engineering and work practice controls come first. Protective equipment is added for any exposure that remains.
Engineering controls remove or isolate the hazard: sharps containers, self-sheathing needles, needles with built-in injury protection, and needleless systems.

Contaminated needles are not bent, recapped or removed, unless the employer shows there is no feasible alternative or a procedure requires it. Even then, only a mechanical device or a one-handed technique is allowed, and shearing or breaking is never allowed.

The exposure control plan is reviewed every year, looking at safer devices with input from frontline staff. After an exposure, the employer must offer a confidential medical evaluation at once, including testing the source blood for hepatitis B and HIV.

scenes.title: Needlestick in a vaccinated worker
scenes.altText: Decision table (ACIP 2018, matching CDC 2013) for HBV after exposure in a health-care worker with a complete vaccine series. Documented responder (anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL after the series): no action needed, whatever the source status. Documented nonresponder after two complete series: source HBsAg positive or unknown → HBIG ×2, one month apart; source negative → no action. Response unknown: test the worker’s anti-HBs and the source’s HBsAg at the same time; anti-HBs ≥10 → no action; anti-HBs <10 with source positive or unknown → HBIG ×1 plus start revaccination; anti-HBs <10 with source negative → one extra vaccine dose and retest 1–2 months later. HBIG is given as soon as possible; its effectiveness after 7 days is unknown. Hook answer card: the isolate stays in the BSC (red flags) and goes to rule-out and referral; the worker is tested for anti-HBs at the same time as the source.

cues.text: Hepatitis B after a needlestick depends on the worker’s documented response. A documented responder, with anti-HBs of at least ten after the series, needs nothing, whatever the source.
A documented nonresponder after two full series gets two doses of hepatitis B immune globulin, a month apart, if the source is positive or unknown.

If the response was never measured, test the worker’s anti-HBs and the source’s surface antigen at the same time. Below ten with a positive or unknown source: one dose of immune globulin and start revaccination. Below ten with a negative source: one extra vaccine dose, then retest.
Back to the hook. The coccobacilli go into the cabinet for rule-out and referral, and the processor is tested for anti-HBs now, with immune globulin given as soon as possible if needed.

props.title: Hook answer
lines: Isolate: BSC, rule out and refer
Worker: anti-HBs now, HBIG fast if needed

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Careful two-handed recapping is acceptable” (✓ recapping is not allowed unless no alternative is feasible, and then only one-handed or with a device); “A vaccinated worker needs nothing after a needlestick” (✓ only a documented responder needs nothing; response unknown means test anti-HBs and the source together); “Identify the suspicious isolate fully before calling anyone” (✓ a sentinel lab rules out and refers to an LRN reference laboratory; reference laboratories test further, national laboratories characterise).

cues.text: Trap one: careful two-handed recapping is fine. No: recapping is not allowed unless there is no feasible alternative, and then only one-handed or with a device.
Trap two: a vaccinated worker needs nothing. No: only a documented responder needs nothing. If the response is unknown, test anti-HBs and the source together.
Trap three: fully identify a suspicious isolate before calling. No: a sentinel lab rules out and refers. Reference labs test further, and national labs characterise.

props.title: ✗ “Careful two-handed recap is fine.”
lines: ✓ No recap; rare exception: one hand or device

scenes.title: Cabinet, cap, check, call
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Four Cs at the bench: CABINET for aerosols and red-flag isolates, no CAP on a used needle, CHECK anti-HBs unless a response is documented, CALL (refer) instead of chasing a possible select agent.” Tokens: Cabinet · No cap · Check anti-HBs · Call and refer. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: four Cs at the bench. Cabinet for aerosols and red-flag isolates. No cap on a used needle. Check anti-HBs unless a response is documented. Call and refer instead of chasing a possible select agent.

Where it breaks: recapping has a narrow one-handed exception; a documented responder needs no check; the BSC does not replace other protection or a risk assessment; and these are US rules, so Philippine requirements may differ.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: US rules; local rules may differ

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Aerosols and red-flag isolates in the BSC · sentinel lab rules out and refers”, “Engineering controls first, no two-handed recapping · needlestick: test anti-HBs unless a response is documented”.

cues.text: Keep aerosol-generating work and red-flag isolates in the biological safety cabinet, rule out and refer a possible select agent rather than identify it, rely on engineered sharps and never recap two-handed, and after a needlestick test anti-HBs unless a protective response is already documented.

props.label: Aerosols + red flags in the BSC · sentinel: rule out and refer
Engineered sharps, no recap · needlestick: anti-HBs unless documented

explanation.what: Plain language: invisible droplets come off many everyday bench steps, so risky work goes into a ventilated cabinet; needles are made safer by design rather than by being careful; a stuck worker who was vaccinated may still need antibody testing; and a hospital lab that suspects a bioterrorism agent stops, keeps it contained and hands it on. Scientific terms: aerosol, biological safety cabinet (BSC), biosafety level (BSL-2, BSL-3), engineering controls, work practice controls, personal protective equipment (PPE), sharps with engineered sharps injury protections, needleless systems, exposure control plan, anti-HBs, hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG), documented responder/nonresponder, Laboratory Response Network (LRN), sentinel/reference/national laboratories, select agent.
explanation.why: Aerosols are often undetectable and come from routine steps, and some dangerous organisms first show up as slow, tiny gram-negative coccobacilli in a routine blood culture. Hazards are best removed at the source, so the law ranks engineering and work practice controls before PPE. Vaccine protection is only known if anti-HBs was measured after the series. Routing suspicious isolates to reference laboratories keeps open-bench workup and exposure to a minimum.
explanation.measure: BSL-2: BSC for specimen processing and aerosol/splash work; BSL-3: BSC for all specimens and cultures. Red flags: tiny slow colonies at 24–48 h with GNR/coccobacilli; blood culture positive ≥48 h; growth only on chocolate agar; boxcar gram-positive rods. OSHA: engineering + work practice controls, then PPE; no bending/recapping/removal unless no alternative is feasible, then one-handed or mechanical; annual plan review. HBV (ACIP 2018): responder ≥10 mIU/mL → no action; nonresponder after 2 series + source +/unknown → HBIG ×2 one month apart; response unknown → test anti-HBs and source together; <10 with source +/unknown → HBIG ×1 + revaccination; <10 with source − → one extra dose and retest; HBIG as soon as possible (effectiveness after 7 days unknown). LRN: sentinel rule out and refer; reference test further; national characterise.
explanation.differs: BSL-2 (BSC for aerosol work) vs BSL-3 (BSC for everything); engineering vs work practice controls vs PPE; documented responder vs nonresponder vs unknown response; sentinel vs reference vs national laboratory.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: pick the engineering control from a list, reject two-handed recapping, choose HBIG plus revaccination for a low-titre worker with an unknown-status source, or pick “keep it in the BSC and refer” for slow-growing gram-negative coccobacilli.

comparisons.title: Engineering vs work practice controls vs PPE

left.label: Engineering + work practice
points: Engineering: safety needles, needleless systems, sharps containers
Work practice: change how a task is done (no two-handed recapping)

right.label: PPE
points: Used for exposure that remains after controls

comparisons.distinguisher: Removing or isolating the hazard vs shielding the worker from what remains.

comparisons.title: Documented responder vs response unknown

left.label: Documented responder
points: Anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL after a complete series
No post-exposure action, whatever the source

right.label: Response unknown
points: Test worker anti-HBs and source HBsAg together

comparisons.distinguisher: Whether protective anti-HBs was ever documented after vaccination.

mnemonic.text: Four Cs at the bench: CABINET for aerosols and red-flag isolates, no CAP on a used needle, CHECK anti-HBs unless a response is documented, CALL (refer) instead of chasing a possible select agent.
mnemonic.explanation: Cabinet = BSC use; Cap = recapping rule; Check = HBV post-exposure testing; Call = sentinel rule-out and referral.
mnemonic.limitation: Recapping has a narrow one-handed or mechanical exception; documented responders need no anti-HBs check; a BSC does not replace PPE or risk assessment; these are US rules and local requirements may differ.

analogyLimitations: Bench and cabinet drawings are schematic.
Regulatory and guideline text is paraphrased (US OSHA, CDC/ACIP only); read the current documents for exact wording.
takeaway: Keep aerosol-generating work and red-flag isolates in the biological safety cabinet, rule out and refer a possible select agent rather than identify it, rely on engineered sharps and never recap two-handed, and after a needlestick test anti-HBs unless a protective response is already documented.

questions.stem: A technologist with written documentation of a complete hepatitis B vaccine series, but no anti-HBs result ever recorded, has a needlestick from a source patient whose HBsAg status cannot be determined. The technologist’s anti-HBs is 4 mIU/mL. What does US ACIP guidance recommend?

options.text: One dose of HBIG and start revaccination as soon as possible
options.rationale: Correct. For a response-unknown worker with anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL and a positive or unknown source, give HBIG ×1 and revaccinate, then check anti-HBs after the last dose.

options.text: No action, because the vaccine series was completed
options.rationale: Incorrect. Only a documented responder (anti-HBs ≥10 mIU/mL after the series) needs no action.

options.text: Two doses of HBIG one month apart and no vaccine
options.rationale: Incorrect. That regimen is for a documented nonresponder after two complete series.

options.text: One extra vaccine dose only, then retest in 1–2 months
options.rationale: Incorrect. That applies when the source is HBsAg-negative; an unknown source is managed like a positive one.

questions.stem: Under the OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard, which of these is an ENGINEERING control?

options.text: A needleless system or a needle with a built-in safety feature
options.rationale: Correct. The standard defines engineering controls as devices that isolate or remove the hazard, including sharps with engineered sharps injury protections and needleless systems.
Incorrect. Gloves are personal protective equipment, used for exposure that remains after controls.

options.text: A rule prohibiting two-handed needle recapping
options.rationale: Incorrect. The standard gives this as its example of a work practice control, which changes how a task is done.

options.text: Offering hepatitis B vaccination to staff with occupational exposure
options.rationale: Incorrect. Making the vaccine available is a separate requirement of the standard (paragraph (f)), not an engineering control.

questions.stem: A hospital (sentinel) laboratory sees tiny, slow-growing colonies from a blood culture that turned positive at 72 hours; the Gram stain shows small gram-negative coccobacilli. The laboratory cannot rule out Brucella. What is the best course?

options.text: Keep all work in the biological safety cabinet and refer the isolate to the LRN reference laboratory
options.rationale: Correct. Gram-negative coccobacilli from blood cultures belong in a BSC, and labs that cannot rule out Brucella or Francisella should consider shipping the isolate to a reference laboratory rather than identifying it.

options.text: Set up an automated identification panel on the open bench to get a species name
options.rationale: Incorrect. Preparing isolates for automated identification generates aerosols, and full workup is not the sentinel role.

options.text: Sniff the plate for a characteristic odour before deciding
options.rationale: Incorrect. CDC recommends that sniffing culture plates be prohibited.

options.text: Report it as a contaminant because it grew slowly
options.rationale: Incorrect. Slow growth of small gram-negative coccobacilli in blood cultures is a red flag for a high-risk pathogen, not a reason to dismiss it.

references.usedFor: Definitions of engineering controls, work practice controls (example: prohibiting two-handed recapping), sharps with engineered sharps injury protections and needleless systems; (d)(2)(i) controls first, PPE for remaining exposure; (d)(2)(vii) no bending/recapping/removal unless no alternative is feasible or a procedure requires it, then mechanical or one-handed technique, shearing/breaking prohibited; (c) annual exposure control plan review with documented consideration of safer devices and frontline input; (f)(3) post-exposure evaluation including source testing.

references.usedFor: LRN-B tiers: sentinel laboratories provide routine diagnostics, rule-out and referral; reference laboratories (about 120 state/local public health, military, veterinary, agriculture and food labs) investigate and/or refer; national laboratories (CDC, USAMRIID, NBFAC) perform specialised characterisation.

claims.text: Aerosol-generating procedures; BSL-2 and BSL-3 BSC use; red-flag isolate features; closed-system analyzers reduce but do not eliminate exposure.
OSHA control hierarchy, engineering control definition, recapping rule and exception, annual plan review, post-exposure evaluation.
HBV post-exposure management by response status and source HBsAg; HBIG timing.
Sentinel rule-out and referral; reference and national laboratory roles; BSC handling and referral of gram-negative coccobacilli; no sniffing of plates.

Select-agent morphology (Hit 47: boxcar non-hemolytic non-motile B. anthracis with Medusa-head colonies, bipolar Y. pestis growing at 28°C, Brucella); “routine closed-specimen chemistry follows standard precautions” as a stand-alone rule.
claims.note: Not taught as facts in this lesson; the lesson only states that closed-system analyzers reduce but do not eliminate exposure.

claims.text: Scenario invented; bench and cabinet drawings schematic.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer’s “check anti-HBs; inadequate titer → HBIG + booster” leaves out context: documented responders need no testing or treatment; documented nonresponders get HBIG ×2; for a response-unknown worker with anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL, management depends on source HBsAg (positive/unknown: HBIG ×1 plus revaccination; negative: one extra vaccine dose and retest), per ACIP 2018 and CDC 2013. The lesson teaches the full table.

The reviewer states that recapping is prohibited; the OSHA standard (29 CFR 1910.1030(d)(2)(vii)) prohibits bending, recapping or removing contaminated needles unless the employer can show no alternative is feasible or a specific procedure requires it, in which case only a mechanical device or one-handed technique may be used. The lesson teaches the rule with its narrow exception.

OSHA, CDC/ACIP and LRN rules taught here are US requirements and structures. Philippine occupational-safety, biosafety and referral rules are not covered; MTLE candidates should check local requirements.
